title: Sleep and food
hookLine: he wrote frankly about his habits of eating and sleeping (Essays 3.13)

lines: WHY PUT THIS IN A BOOK?
cards: A philosopher at dinner bites his own tongue. Sometimes his fingers. He eats too fast, he admits.
He loves sauces, though his father hated them. Salads and fruit, not much, except melons. He can manage without a tablecloth, but a clean napkin he really wants.
This isn't a servant's gossip. It's Montaigne, writing about himself in Of experience, the closing essay of his book. Why would a serious writer put his napkins next to his thoughts on death and God?

teach.h: A HARD BED, A HURRIED MEAL.
teach.b: First, the plain facts, given plainly. Sleep, he says, has taken up a large part of his life. He likes his bed hard, and he likes to sleep alone, well covered.
He eats greedily and in a hurry. He knows which foods agree with him and which habits he'd do better to break. He isn't confessing.
He's reporting, the way you'd describe the weather. Second, the reason. Nature, Montaigne says, has been like a mother here.

The things we have to do to stay alive, she made pleasant too, and she calls us to them not only through reason but through appetite. Eating and sleeping aren't a tax paid before the real life starts.
They're part of the gift. Third, his quarrel. Some people count an act as less worthy because it's necessary, as if eating and sleeping were beneath a serious mind.

Nobody, he says, will get it out of his head that pleasure and necessity make a very fitting marriage. He wants the mind to keep the body company at the table, not sit apart from it, sniffing. Fourth, an ordinary day.

teach.h: THE BOWL, THE WATER, THE BED.
teach.b: A warm bowl of something when you're cold.

teach.h: ORDINARY PLEASURES ARE PART OF THE GIFT.
teach.b: The first sip of water when you're thirsty. Lying down at night and feeling the weight leave your feet. Montaigne would count every one, not as the reward for a day well spent, but as the day itself, being lived.
A man who wrote down so many doubts still thought a good night's sleep belonged in the book.

how: Readers of Montaigne often take the eating and sleeping passages of Of experience as permission to treat daily needs as part of a good life rather than a distraction from it; some use them as a cue to eat one meal a day without hurry.

o: a list of foods every reader should avoid
a strict diet and rest plan for a disciplined mind
Montaigne's view that our daily needs are part of the gift

games.q: inside sleep and food: tap the pairs.
p: he bites his tongue, even his fingers

s: Montaigne kept his eating and sleeping habits out of his book
he describes them plainly, in the closing essay, Of experience.
he says nature calls us to our needs through appetite, not only reason
the things we need to do, she made pleasant too.
he thought an act was less worthy because it was necessary
he says pleasure and necessity make a very fitting marriage.

games.q: you're Montaigne, writing a serious book about how to live. do you include how you eat and sleep?
o: yes, plainly, because it's part of living.
games.why: he puts them right in the closing essay, next to his thoughts on experience, because he thinks nature made our needs pleasant on purpose.

practice: Enjoy one ordinary pleasure, on purpose: if there's a drink nearby, take a slow sip and actually taste it, and if not, notice the pleasure already here, the chair holding you up, warm hands, a full breath going all the way down.
Stay with the one you pick, and when your mind wanders off to the list, bring it back. No need to make it deep; just let it be pleasant.

wordCard.voice: Sleep and food. Montaigne's frank account of his own eating and sleeping, and his claim that nature made our needs pleasant on purpose. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: ordinary pleasures. The bowl, the water and the bed all count. Until tomorrow.
